claim.pdf_says: When an operand is textually subscripted, as operand-j<sub>n</sub>, the term 'operand-j' identifies a specific operand and 'n' refers to the nth position or occurrence of operand-j.
claim.markdown_says: When an operand is textually subscripted, as operand-jn, the term 'operand-j' identifies a specific operand and 'n' refers to the nth position or occurrence of operand-j.
claim.why_it_matters: The subscript n is printed as a subscript in the PDF; the markdown flattens it to 'operand-jn', so the very notation 5.3.1 defines is not shown (it reads as a different operand name).

verdict.reasoning: Rendered printed page 20 (PDF p42) at 300 dpi: §2002:5.3.1 reads 'as operand-j' followed by a lowered, smaller 'n' (a true subscript glyph). page-42.md line 9 reads 'as operand-jn' with the n on the baseline, no subscript markup. Both sources are quoted accurately by the claim. Ordinarily lost subscript styling is mere formatting, but here the subscript IS the content: 5.3.1 exists to define the textual-subscript notation, and the flattened 'operand-jn' is indistinguishable from an operand named 'operand-jn', so the defining example no longer shows the notation it defines. Genuine but cosmetic transcription loss; no normative rule text is missing.
